flawed_step: The claim that k = ceil(n/2) makes every k-Opt local optimum globally optimal fails already at n = 8, k = 4.
counterexample: n=8, k=4. Weights: w(12)=w(23)=w(45)=w(56)=w(78)=10; w(34)=w(67)=w(18)=0; w(13)=w(25)=w(46)=w(57)=w(28)=9; every other edge 100. T=1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8-1 has cost 50. T'=1-3-4-6-7-5-2-8-1 has cost 45 and differs from T in 5 edges. T is 4-opt: (i) a tour using a weight-100 edge costs >=100; (ii) a tour missing one of 34, 67, 18 has at least 6 edges of weight >=9, so cost >=54; (iii) a tour S containing 34, 67 and 18 gives C = (weight-10 edges S drops) + (weight-9 edges S adds), and C is balanced at every vertex. Balance at vertices 1,3,4,6,7,8 forces C to take all or none of each group {12,13,23}, {45,46,56}, {57,78,28}; call these X, Z, W and the edge 25 Y. Vertex 2 gives 2X=Y+W and vertex 5 gives 2Z=Y+W, so all are 0 or all are 1. Hence S=T or S=T', and T' is 5 edges away. So T is a 4-Opt local optimum (cost 50) but not optimal (T' costs 45).
assessment_summary: Counterexample at n=8, k=4. The weight-0 edges shared by T and T' are forced into any cheap neighbour. The edges where the tours differ form one alternating structure with no proper balanced part. So the only cheap tours are T and T', and they differ in 5 > 4 edges. T is 4-opt with cost 50, while T' costs 45.
